#### Beyond the United States

The International Labour Organization (ILO) estimates the employment-population ratio of almost every
country in the same way, for people aged 15 and over. The World Bank publishes these estimates, which start
in 1991. A wider file holds them, one row per country and year.

```{python}
# Load the ILO estimates: one row per country and year
world_emp = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "emp_pop_countries.csv")
world_emp.head()
```

These are annual *model estimates*: where a country has no labor survey in a year, the ILO fills the gap
with a statistical model. For the United States they run about 0.7 points below the BLS ratio above,
because the ILO counts people from age 15 (the BLS from 16).

First the data: `emp_pop_latest` picks the rows of the chosen countries, and each
country's ratio in the latest year, which the title reports.

```{python}
# The countries of the picker, A to Z, and each country's World Bank region:
# `dict(zip(a, b))` pairs each country with its region
EMP_COUNTRIES = sorted(world_emp.country.unique())
EMP_REGIONS = dict(zip(world_emp.country, world_emp.region))


def emp_pop_latest(names):
    """The rows of the chosen countries, and their ratios in the latest year (Fig. 1).

    Arguments
        names : the countries to show
    Returns
        chosen : their rows of world_emp
        last   : the latest year of those rows
        latest : each country's employment-population ratio in that year
    """
    # Step 1: `.isin(names)` is True for the rows of the chosen countries
    chosen = world_emp[world_emp.country.isin(names)]
    # Step 2: the latest year, and each country's ratio in it (country -> percent)
    last = chosen.year.max()
    latest = chosen[chosen.year == last].set_index("country").emp_pop_ratio
    return chosen, last, latest
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 1 for any countries, ages 15+
# the website's default view, and one fixed color per country (group_colors)
EMP_SHOWN = ["United States", "Germany", "Japan"]
EMP_COLORS = group_colors(
    EMP_SHOWN + EMP_COUNTRIES,
    region_groups(EMP_REGIONS, EMP_SHOWN),
    BOOK_COLORS,
)


def emp_pop_countries(names=("United States",)):
    """The employment-population ratio, ages 15+, of any countries (ILO estimates).

    Draws Fig. 1 for any countries (inspired by Fig. 7.1 in Jones), with the highest
    and the lowest ratio of the latest year in the title.

    Arguments
        names : the countries to draw
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the data (emp_pop_latest); a message when no country is picked
    chosen, last, latest = emp_pop_latest(names)
    if len(chosen) == 0:
        return go.Figure(layout=dict(title="Pick at least one country"))
    # Step 2: the title, the highest ratio first and the lowest second
    title = (
        f"Share of adults with a job in {last}: "
        f"{latest.idxmax()} {latest.max():.1f}%"
    )
    if len(latest) > 1:
        title = title + f", {latest.idxmin()} {latest.min():.1f}%"
    # Step 3: one line per country; `color_discrete_map` gives each line its
    # fixed color
    fig = px.line(
        chosen,
        x="year",
        y="emp_pop_ratio",
        color="country",
        hover_name="country",
        color_discrete_map=EMP_COLORS,
        title=title,
        labels={
            "year": "Year",
            "emp_pop_ratio": "Employed, % of population 15+",
            "country": "Country",
        },
    )
    # Step 4: the U.S. range, or one wider range for countries far from the U.S.
    low, high = 50, 66
    if chosen.emp_pop_ratio.min() < low or chosen.emp_pop_ratio.max() > high:
        low, high = 15, 90
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[low, high])
    # no tick label in the bottom-left corner
    fig.update_xaxes(
        range=[1990, 2026],
        tickvals=[1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2025],
    )
    return fig
```

Below, Colab shows a country picker. On the website, the chart holds every country: **pick a region in the menu,
then click a country in the legend to add it.**

```{python}
# at the end only hides an extra line of text.
```

**Sources.** Data: International Labour Organization, modelled estimates, published in the
[World Bank, World Development Indicators, Employment to population ratio, 15+, total (`SL.EMP.TOTL.SP.ZS`)](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SL.EMP.TOTL.SP.ZS).
Prepared file: [`data/ch07/emp_pop_countries.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch07/emp_pop_countries.csv)
(see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch07/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 7.1 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

The next cell checks the numbers of What to notice: five countries in 2000 and 2025,
and the lowest and the highest ratios of 2025.

```{python}
# The ratios as a wide table: `.pivot(...)` turns the long table into one row per
# year and one column per country
ratios = world_emp.pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="emp_pop_ratio")
print(
    ratios.loc[[2000, 2025], ["United States", "Germany", "Japan", "France", "Italy"]]
)
# `.dropna()` drops the empty cells, and `.iloc[[0, 1, 2, -3, -2, -1]]` picks rows
# by position (`-1` is the last): the three lowest and the three highest of 2025
print(ratios.loc[2025].dropna().sort_values().iloc[[0, 1, 2, -3, -2, -1]])
```

**What to notice.**

- Add **Germany** and **Japan**. Between 2000 and 2025 the U.S. ratio fell from 63.5 to 59.1 percent, while
  Germany's rose from 53.4 to 58.3 and Japan's from 59.5 to 61.9. Japan now employs a larger share of its
  adults than the United States.
- Add **France** and **Italy**: 51.2 and 46.2 percent in 2025, far below the U.S. ratio throughout.
- **Look at your data.** The highest ratios (above 82 percent) are in Qatar, whose residents are mostly
  migrant workers, and in poor countries such as Madagascar and Tanzania, where few people can afford not to
  work. The lowest (21 to 27 percent) are in São Tomé and Príncipe, Djibouti, Yemen and Somalia. Where
  surveys are rare, these numbers come mostly from the ILO's model, so treat them with care.

### Fig. 2: The U.S. unemployment rate

**Goal.** See how unemployment jumps in recessions and falls in recoveries.

A person is **unemployed** when she has no job, has looked for one in the past four weeks, and is
available to work. The **labor force** is everybody who is employed or unemployed, and the
**unemployment rate** is the share of the labor force that is unemployed.

```{python}
# Load the data of Fig. 2: the monthly U.S. unemployment rate
unrate = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig7-2.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
```

```{python}

    unrate,
    x="date",
    y="unemployment_rate",
    hover_name="date",
    labels={"date": "Year", "unemployment_rate": "Unemployment rate (%)"},
    title="Unemployment jumps in every recession and falls slowly afterwards",
)
fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=2))
# Step 2: the shaded bands: every recession since 1950
shade_recessions(fig, "1950-01-01")
# Step 3: no tick label in the bottom-left corner, and the range slider below

fig.update_xaxes(rangeslider_visible=True)
fig.show()
```

**Sources.** Data: [U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Population Survey, Unemployment Rate (`UNRATE`), via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/UNRATE);
recession dates: [NBER, U.S. Business Cycle Expansions and Contractions](https://www.nber.org/research/data/us-business-cycle-expansions-and-contractions),
via the FRED recession indicator [`USREC`](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/USREC).
Prepared files: [`data/ch07/fig7-2.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch07/fig7-2.csv), [`data/ch07/recessions.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch07/recessions.csv)
(see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch07/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 7.2 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- Every shaded recession brings a jump in unemployment. The highest peaks are late 1982, October 2009
  and April 2020.
- The Covid-19 jump was the largest and the shortest: the rate fell back much faster than after 2009.
- Between recessions, unemployment falls gradually, often for many years.

<!-- cell -->

#### Key numbers: peaks and recoveries

```{python}
# The key numbers of Fig. 2: the rates, with the months as row labels
u = unrate.set_index("date").unemployment_rate
print(
    f"May 2007: {u.loc['2007-05-01']:.1f}%   "
    f"October 2009: {u.loc['2009-10-01']:.1f}%"
)
print(
    f"February 2020: {u.loc['2020-02-01']:.1f}%   "
    f"April 2020: {u.loc['2020-04-01']:.1f}%"
)
# the months after each peak; `after_2009[after_2009 < 4]` keeps the months below
# 4 percent, and `.index[0]` is the first of them
after_2009 = u.loc["2009-11":]
after_2020 = u.loc["2020-05":]
print(f"First month below 4% after 2009:  {after_2009[after_2009 < 4].index[0]:%B %Y}")
print(f"First month below 4% after 2020:  {after_2020[after_2020 < 4].index[0]:%B %Y}")
```

The rates match the textbook, except April 2020: 14.8 percent in today's data, against 14.7 in the
textbook (seasonal adjustment is revised every year). After the 2009 peak it took until May 2018,
almost nine years, to get below 4 percent again. After the Covid peak it took until December 2021,
under two years.

#### Table 7.1: the composition of the U.S. labor force

A wider file holds the monthly levels behind the unemployment rate, in millions of people. We rebuild
Table 7.1 for January 2023, the textbook's month, and for the latest month.

```{python}
# Step 1: the monthly levels in millions, with the dates as row labels, and the
# unemployment rate computed from them
force = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "labor_force.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
force = force.set_index("date")
force["unemployment_rate"] = 100 * force.unemployed / force.labor_force
# Step 2: `.loc[[...]]` picks two rows by their dates (January 2023 and the latest
# month), and `.T` transposes the table: each month becomes a column
last = force.index[-1]
table = force.loc[[pd.Timestamp("2023-01-01"), last]].T
table.columns = ["January 2023", f"{last:%B %Y}"]
# Step 3: the textbook's numbers, for comparison
table["Textbook (Jan. 2023)"] = [266, 166, 160, 5.7, 100, 3.4]
table.round(2)
```

January 2023 agrees with the textbook within rounding, except that today's data count 5.77 million
unemployed (the textbook says 5.7), so the rate is 3.48 rather than 3.4 percent. By the latest month,
the labor force has grown to about 170 million and unemployment to about 4.2 percent.

The textbook also notes that, with about 266 million people aged 16 and over, one point of the
employment-population ratio is 2.7 million jobs:

```{python}
# One percent of the population aged 16 and over, in millions of people
print(
    "1% of the population 16+, January 2023: "
    f"{0.01 * force.loc['2023-01-01', 'population']:.2f} million people"
)
print(
    f"1% of the population 16+, {last:%B %Y}:  "
    f"{0.01 * force.loc[last, 'population']:.2f} million people"
)
```

#### Beyond the United States

The OECD publishes *harmonised* unemployment rates: every country counts the unemployed with the same
definition as the United States (no job, looking for one, available to work). A wider file holds the monthly
rates of 34 OECD countries, from the FRED database.

```{python}
# Load the monthly rates of 34 OECD countries. `groupby("country").date.min()`
# gives each country's first month; the five latest starts come last
monthly = pd.read_csv(
    DATA_URL + "unemployment_countries_monthly.csv",
    parse_dates=["date"],
)
monthly.groupby("country").date.min().sort_values().tail()
```

The series start at different dates: Canada, Japan and the United States in 1955, most of Europe in the
1980s, Germany in 1991 (after reunification), Turkey in 2005 and Israel in 2012. New Zealand and Switzerland
publish only quarterly rates. The U.S. rows are the BLS rate of the chart above.

First the data: `unemployment_peak` picks the rows of the chosen countries and finds
the highest monthly rate among them, which the title reports.

```{python}
# The countries of the picker, A to Z
MONTHLY_COUNTRIES = sorted(monthly.country.unique())


def unemployment_peak(names):
    """The monthly rates of the chosen countries, and the highest of them (Fig. 2).

    Arguments
        names : the countries to show
    Returns
        chosen : their rows of monthly
        peak   : the row of the highest rate (its country, date and rate)
    """
    # Step 1: the rows of the chosen countries
    chosen = monthly[monthly.country.isin(names)]
    if len(chosen) == 0:
        return chosen, None                    # nothing chosen: no peak
    # Step 2: `.idxmax()` gives the row label of the highest rate, and `.loc[...]`
    # picks that whole row, so `peak.country` and `peak.date` say where and when
    peak = chosen.loc[chosen.unemployment_rate.idxmax()]
    return chosen, peak
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 2 for OECD countries
# the website's default view, and one fixed color per country (group_colors)
MONTHLY_SHOWN = ["United States", "Germany"]
MONTHLY_COLORS = group_colors(
    MONTHLY_SHOWN + MONTHLY_COUNTRIES,
    [MONTHLY_SHOWN, MONTHLY_COUNTRIES],
    BOOK_COLORS,
)


def unemployment_countries(names=("United States",)):
    """The monthly harmonised unemployment rates of OECD countries.

    Draws Fig. 2 for any OECD countries (inspired by Fig. 7.2 in Jones), with the
    highest rate in the title.

    Arguments
        names : the countries to draw
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the data (unemployment_peak); a message when no country is picked
    chosen, peak = unemployment_peak(names)
    if len(chosen) == 0:
        return go.Figure(layout=dict(title="Pick at least one country"))
    # Step 2: one line per country, in its fixed color
    fig = px.line(
        chosen,
        x="date",
        y="unemployment_rate",
        color="country",
        hover_name="country",
        color_discrete_map=MONTHLY_COLORS,
        title=(
            f"Highest rate: {peak.country}, {peak.unemployment_rate:.1f}% "
            f"in {peak.date:%B %Y}"
        ),
        labels={
            "date": "Year",
            "unemployment_rate": "Unemployment rate (%)",
            "country": "Country",
        },
    )
    # Step 3: 0 to 16 percent, widened only for very high rates; the range slider
    high = 16 if chosen.unemployment_rate.max() <= 16 else 30
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, high])
    fig.update_xaxes(rangeslider_visible=True)
    return fig
```

## Supply and demand in the labor market

Now the model. We draw the labor market, add an income tax, and let labor demand fall, first with a flexible wage and then with a wage that does not adjust.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 3: The labor market

**Goal.** Draw the supply-and-demand diagram of the labor market and see how its equilibrium moves.

Labor demand $w = \bar{a}_d - \bar{b}_d L$ slopes down and labor supply $w = \bar{a}_s + \bar{b}_s L$
slopes up. They cross at $(L^*, w^*)$, equation (3). If the population is a fixed number $N$, the model also gives
the employment-population ratio $L^*/N$. When you move a slider, the starting curves stay on the chart
as dashed gray lines, so you can see the shift.

The function below draws the diagram. It needs only `equilibrium` and the two lines
of "Model in code", so all of its code is drawing code.

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 3, the labor market
def labor_market(a_d=100.0, b_d=1.0, a_s=10.0, b_s=1.0):
    """Labor supply, labor demand and the equilibrium where they cross.

    Draws Fig. 3 (adapted from Fig. 7.3 in Jones). Once a parameter differs from
    Islandia's, the starting lines stay on the chart as dashed gray lines.

    Arguments
        a_d, b_d : intercept and slope of labor demand, a-bar_d and b-bar_d
        a_s, b_s : intercept and slope of labor supply, a-bar_s and b-bar_s
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the equilibrium, equation (3)
    L_star, w_star = equilibrium(a_d, b_d, a_s, b_s)
    # Step 2: the two lines; demand is labeled at its top-left end (`start=True`)
    fig = go.Figure()
    add_curve(fig, labor_supply(L_grid, a_s, b_s), "Lˢ", TEAL)
    add_curve(fig, labor_demand(L_grid, a_d, b_d), "Lᵈ", BLUE, start=True)
    # Step 3: the starting lines in dashed gray, once a parameter has moved
    if (a_d, b_d, a_s, b_s) != (100.0, 1.0, 10.0, 1.0):
        add_curve(fig, labor_supply(L_grid), "", GRAY, "dash")
        add_curve(fig, labor_demand(L_grid), "", GRAY, "dash")
    # Step 4: the equilibrium point, and a title with the wage and employment
    add_point(fig, L_star, w_star, "")
    return market_axes(
        fig,
        f"The labor market clears at w* = {w_star:.1f} and L* = {L_star:.1f}",
    )
```

**What to notice.**

- With our illustrative numbers the market clears at $L^* = 45$ and $w^* = 55$.
- A higher $\bar{a}_d$ (firms value every worker more) shifts demand up: the wage **and** employment rise.
- A higher $\bar{a}_s$ (people need a higher wage before they work) shifts supply up: the wage rises but
  employment **falls**.
- Steeper curves (larger slopes) make employment respond less to a given shift.

### Fig. 4: An income tax at rate τ

**Goal.** See how a tax on labor income lowers employment and drives a wedge between the wage
firms pay and the wage workers keep.

With a tax at rate $\tau$, a worker keeps only $(1-\tau)w$ of the wage $w$ the firm pays. To supply the
same amount of work as before, workers now need a higher wage from the firm, $w = (\bar{a}_s + \bar{b}_s L)/(1-\tau)$.
Drawn against the wage firms pay, labor supply shifts **back** (up and to the left). The economy moves
from $A$ to $B$ (equation 4).

First we compute the numbers the figure reports. `tax_wedge` solves the market
without the tax (point $A$) and with it (point $B$), and the wage workers keep at $B$.

```{python}
def tax_wedge(tau, b_s):
    """The labor market without (A) and with (B) a tax on labor income (Fig. 4).

    Equations (3) and (4): workers keep (1 - tau) w of the wage w that firms pay

    Arguments
        tau : tax rate on labor income
        b_s : slope of labor supply, b-bar_s
    Returns
        L_A, w_A : employment and the wage at A, without the tax
        L_B, w_B : employment and the wage firms pay at B, with the tax
        kept     : the wage workers keep at B, (1 - tau) w_B
    """
    # Step 1: the equilibrium without and with the tax
    L_A, w_A = equilibrium(b_s=b_s)
    L_B, w_B = equilibrium(b_s=b_s, tau=tau)
    # Step 2: what workers keep at B; the gap w_B - kept is the tax per unit of work
    kept = (1 - tau) * w_B
    return L_A, w_A, L_B, w_B, kept
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 4, an income tax
def income_tax(tau=0.25, b_s=1.0):
    """A tax on labor income shifts labor supply back; the economy moves from A to B.

    Draws Fig. 4 (adapted from Fig. 7.4 in Jones), with the tax wedge as a green bar.

    Arguments
        tau : tax rate on labor income
        b_s : slope of labor supply, b-bar_s
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the numbers of the figure (tax_wedge)
    L_A, w_A, L_B, w_B, kept = tax_wedge(tau, b_s)
    # Step 2: the taxed supply line (the wage firms must pay is the old one divided
    # by 1 - tau), the old one dashed, and demand
    fig = go.Figure()
    taxed = add_curve(fig, labor_supply(L_grid, b_s=b_s) / (1 - tau), "Lˢ′", TEAL)
    add_curve(fig, labor_supply(L_grid, b_s=b_s), "Lˢ", GRAY, "dash", avoid=taxed)
    add_curve(fig, labor_demand(L_grid), "Lᵈ", BLUE, start=True)
    # Step 3: the points A and B; with no tax, B is the same point as A
    add_point(fig, L_A, w_A, "A")
    if tau > 0:
        add_point(fig, L_B, w_B, "B")
    # Step 4: the green bar at B, from the wage workers keep up to the wage firms pay
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=[L_B, L_B],
            y=[kept, w_B],
            mode="lines+markers",
            name="Tax wedge",
            showlegend=True,
            line=dict(color=GREEN, width=6),
        )
    )
    title = (
        f"τ = {tau:.0%}: L′ = {L_B:.1f}, firms pay w′ = {w_B:.1f}, "
        f"workers keep {kept:.1f}"
    )
    return market_axes(fig, title, y_title="Wage paid by firms, w")
```

### Fig. 5: A reduction in labor demand

**Goal.** See what happens to the wage and employment when firms want fewer workers.

New rules that make firing workers costly, or a jump in the price of an input such as oil, can make
firms less willing to hire. In the diagram, labor demand shifts down by an amount we call `shift`:
$w = (\bar{a}_d - \text{shift}) - \bar{b}_d L$. The economy moves from $A$ to $B$.

The function below draws the diagram. It needs only the two equilibria of equation
(3), from `equilibrium`, so all of its code is drawing code.

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 5, a reduction in labor demand
def demand_fall(shift=20.0, b_s=1.0):
    """Labor demand shifts back by `shift`; the wage and employment both fall.

    Draws Fig. 5 (adapted from Fig. 7.5 in Jones): the economy moves from A to B.

    Arguments
        shift : the fall in labor demand (its intercept falls from 100 to 100 - shift)
        b_s   : slope of labor supply, b-bar_s
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the old and the new equilibrium, equation (3)
    L_A, w_A = equilibrium(b_s=b_s)
    L_B, w_B = equilibrium(a_d=100 - shift, b_s=b_s)
    # Step 2: the new demand line, the old one dashed, and supply
    fig = go.Figure()
    after = add_curve(fig, labor_demand(L_grid, 100 - shift), "Lᵈ′", BLUE, start=True)
    add_curve(fig, labor_demand(L_grid), "Lᵈ", GRAY, "dash", start=True, avoid=after)
    add_curve(fig, labor_supply(L_grid, b_s=b_s), "Lˢ", TEAL)
    # Step 3: the points A and B; with no fall, B is the same point as A
    add_point(fig, L_A, w_A, "A")
    if shift > 0:
        add_point(fig, L_B, w_B, "B")
        # a black arrow at L = 60, from the old demand line down to the new one.
        # `add_annotation` with `showarrow=True` draws an arrow from (ax, ay) to
        # (x, y); with `axref="x"` and `ayref="y"` both points are in axis units
        fig.add_annotation(
            x=60,
            y=labor_demand(60, 100 - shift) + 1,
            ax=60,
            ay=labor_demand(60) - 1,
            xref="x",
            yref="y",
            axref="x",
            ayref="y",
            text="",
            showarrow=True,
            arrowhead=3,
            arrowwidth=2,
            arrowcolor="black",
        )
    return market_axes(
        fig,
        (
            f"Demand falls by {shift:.0f}: w {w_A:.1f} → {w_B:.1f}, "
            f"L {L_A:.1f} → {L_B:.1f}"
        ),
    )
```

### Fig. 6: A reduction in labor demand with wage rigidity

**Goal.** See why a wage that does not fall turns a fall in demand into a much larger fall in employment.

Suppose the wage stays at its old level $\bar{w} = w^*$ after labor demand falls. Firms then hire only
what they want at $\bar{w}$, so employment moves along the new demand curve to $C$ (equation 5):

$$L'' = \frac{(\bar{a}_d - \text{shift}) - \bar{w}}{\bar{b}_d}$$

At $\bar{w}$, the number of people who want to work is still $L^*$, so $L^* - L''$ people would like a job
but cannot find one. In Colab, choose **rigid** or **flexible** with the buttons to compare $C$ with $B$; the website version shows the rigid wage.

First we compute the three points of the figure. `rigid_wage` finds $B$ (flexible
wage), $C$ (rigid wage), and the people who want a job at $\bar{w}$ but have none.

```{python}
def rigid_wage(shift):
    """Employment after a fall in labor demand: flexible and rigid wage (Fig. 6).

    Equations (3) and (5): with a flexible wage the market clears again at B; with a
    rigid wage w-bar = w*, firms hire L'' = ((a_d - shift) - w-bar) / b_d, point C

    Arguments
        shift : the fall in labor demand
    Returns
        L_A, w_bar : employment and the wage before the fall (A); w* sets w-bar
        L_B, w_B   : employment and the wage with a flexible wage (B)
        L_C        : employment with the rigid wage (C)
        jobless    : the people who want to work at w-bar but have no job
    """
    # Step 1: A, the old equilibrium, sets the rigid wage w-bar
    L_A, w_bar = equilibrium()
    # Step 2: B, with a flexible wage; C, firms' demand at w-bar
    L_B, w_B = equilibrium(a_d=100 - shift)
    L_C = demand_at_wage(w_bar, a_d=100 - shift)
    # Step 3: want to work at w-bar (labor supply), minus the jobs at C
    jobless = supply_at_wage(w_bar) - L_C
    return L_A, w_bar, L_B, w_B, L_C, jobless
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 6, a reduction in labor demand with wage rigidity
def wage_rigidity(shift=20.0, wage="rigid"):
    """Labor demand falls; with a rigid wage w-bar the economy moves to C, not to B.

    Draws Fig. 6 (adapted from Fig. 7.6 in Jones).

    Arguments
        shift : the fall in labor demand
        wage  : "rigid" (point C, with the jobless gap) or "flexible" (point B)
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the numbers of the figure (rigid_wage)
    L_A, w_bar, L_B, w_B, L_C, jobless = rigid_wage(shift)
    # Step 2: the new demand line, the old one dashed, and supply; the point A
    fig = go.Figure()
    after = add_curve(fig, labor_demand(L_grid, 100 - shift), "Lᵈ′", BLUE, start=True)
    add_curve(fig, labor_demand(L_grid), "Lᵈ", GRAY, "dash", start=True, avoid=after)
    add_curve(fig, labor_supply(L_grid), "Lˢ", TEAL)
    add_point(fig, L_A, w_bar, "A")
    # Step 3, rigid wage: the point C, and a green bar from C to A at w-bar
    # (with no fall, C is the same point as A)
    if wage == "rigid":
        if shift > 0:
            add_point(fig, L_C, w_bar, "C")
        fig.add_trace(
            go.Scatter(
                x=[L_C, L_A],
                y=[w_bar, w_bar],
                mode="lines",
                name="Want a job, cannot find one",
                showlegend=True,
                line=dict(color=GREEN, width=6),
            )
        )
        title = (
            f"Rigid wage w̄ = {w_bar:.1f}: L″ = {L_C:.1f} "
            f"(flexible: L′ = {L_B:.1f}); jobless gap {jobless:.1f}"
        )
    # Step 3, flexible wage: the point B (with no fall, the same point as A)
    else:
        if shift > 0:
            add_point(fig, L_B, w_B, "B")
        title = (
            f"Flexible wage: the wage falls to w′ = {w_B:.1f} "
            f"and employment to L′ = {L_B:.1f}"
        )
    return market_axes(fig, title)
```

**Source.** Adapted from Fig. 7.6 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- With a flexible wage, a fall in demand of 20 moves the economy to $B$: employment 35. With the wage
  stuck at $\bar{w} = 55$ it moves to $C$: employment 25, twice the fall.
- At $C$, 45 people want to work at the going wage but only 25 are hired: a gap of 20. Wage rigidity
  creates unemployment that a flexible wage would not.
- This is the reason Keynes gave for the mass unemployment of the Great Depression, and rigid wages
  return in the short-run chapters of the book.

<!-- cell -->

#### The bathtub model of unemployment

The textbook's Section 7.4 explains the **natural rate of unemployment** with a simple model. The labor
force $\bar{L}$ is fixed, and each month a share $\bar{s}$ of the employed lose their job (the **job
separation rate**) while a share $\bar{f}$ of the unemployed find one (the **job finding rate**),
as in equation (6):

$$E_t + U_t = \bar{L} \qquad\qquad \Delta U_{t+1} = \bar{s}E_t - \bar{f}U_t$$

Unemployment is like water in a bathtub: job losses are the faucet and job findings the drain. The level
stops changing when the two flows are equal, which gives the steady-state rate of equation (7)

$$u^* = \frac{\bar{s}}{\bar{f} + \bar{s}}$$

First the economics: `bathtub_simulation` applies equation (6) month by month for five
years, and computes the natural rate of equation (7).

```{python}
def bathtub_simulation(s, f):
    """The bathtub model: 60 months of unemployment, starting at 10 percent.

    Equation (6) once a month, E + U = L-bar and U' = U + s E - f U, and the
    natural rate of equation (7), u* = s / (f + s)

    Arguments
        s : monthly job separation rate, s-bar
        f : monthly job finding rate, f-bar
    Returns
        path   : a table with the month (0 to 60) and the unemployment rate (percent)
        u_star : the natural rate of unemployment, in percent
    """
    # Step 1: the labor force and the unemployed (only their ratio matters)
    L_bar, U = 100.0, 10.0
    # Step 2: `range(61)` counts 0, 1, ..., 60, one step per month. Each pass
    # stores the month and the current rate with `.append` (which adds one item to
    # the end of a list), then applies equation (6) once
    months, rates = [], []
    for t in range(61):
        months.append(t)
        rates.append(100 * U / L_bar)
        E = L_bar - U                          # the labor force: E + U = L_bar
        U = U + s * E - f * U                  # equation (6)
    # Step 3: the natural rate, equation (7), and the path as a table
    u_star = 100 * s / (f + s)
    path = pd.DataFrame({"month": months, "rate": rates})
    return path, u_star
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: the bathtub model of unemployment
def bathtub_path(s=0.01, f=0.20):
    """Unemployment month by month, and the natural rate it settles at.

    Draws the bathtub figure of this section (our own figure: the textbook draws none
    for Section 7.4), with the natural rate u* as a dashed line.

    Arguments
        s : monthly job separation rate, s-bar
        f : monthly job finding rate, f-bar
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the simulation (bathtub_simulation)
    path, u_star = bathtub_simulation(s, f)
    # Step 2: the path, and the natural rate as a dashed line
    fig = px.line(
        path,
        x="month",
        y="rate",
        hover_name="month",
        labels={
            "month": "Months from the start",
            "rate": "Unemployment rate (percent)",
        },
        title=(
            f"s = {s:.3f}, f = {f:.2f}: unemployment settles at "
            f"u* = s/(f+s) = {u_star:.1f}%"
        ),
    )
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3))
    fig.add_hline(y=u_star, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    # Step 3: one tick a year (no label in the bottom-left corner), and 0 to 25%
    fig.update_xaxes(tickvals=[12, 24, 36, 48, 60])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 25])
    return fig
```

With the textbook's monthly rates, $\bar{s} = 0.01$ and $\bar{f} = 0.20$, the natural rate is
$0.01/0.21 \approx 4.8$ percent. Starting from 10 percent, unemployment is already close to it after a
year, because a fifth of the unemployed find a job every month.

```{python}
# The natural rate, equation (7), for three pairs of rates: the textbook's, and
# two with firing costs; `:<6` pads a number to 6 characters, so the columns line up
for s, f in [[0.01, 0.20], [0.008, 0.20], [0.008, 0.15]]:
    print(f"s = {s:<6} f = {f:<5} natural rate u* = {100 * s / (f + s):.2f}%")
```

The textbook warns that firing costs cut job losses ($\bar{s}$ falls) but can also make firms slow to
hire ($\bar{f}$ falls). In the second line, firing costs only lower $\bar{s}$, and the natural rate falls to
3.85 percent. In the third line they also lower $\bar{f}$, and the natural rate rises to 5.06 percent.

## Unemployment around the world

Unemployment in Europe was once lower than in the United States and then rose well above it. We compare the three large economies and many more.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 7: Unemployment in the United States, Europe and Japan

**Goal.** Compare unemployment in three large economies, and see when Europe's rate rose above the
U.S. rate.

The file has annual rates. "Europe" is the euro area of 12 countries from the European Commission's
AMECO database, which starts in 1960. The textbook uses an OECD series instead, which runs up to
about 1 point higher in the mid-1980s.

```{python}
# Load the data of Fig. 7, and give the columns the economies' names
unemp = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig7-7.csv")
unemp = unemp.rename(
    columns={
        "unrate_us": "United States",
        "unrate_europe": "Europe",
        "unrate_japan": "Japan",
    }
)
unemp.head(7)
```

The empty cells (`NaN`, "not a number") are the years 1955–1959, before the European series starts.

`rates_in` picks the three rates of one year, which the title of the figure reports.

```{python}
def rates_in(year):
    """The unemployment rates of the three economies in one year (Fig. 7).

    Arguments
        year : the year, 1955 to 2025
    Returns
        the row of unemp for that year (its columns are the three economies)
    """
    # `unemp[unemp.year == year]` keeps the rows where the condition is true, and
    # `.iloc[0]` takes the first of them
    return unemp[unemp.year == year].iloc[0]
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 7, unemployment in three economies
def unemployment_in(year=2022):
    """Unemployment in the U.S., Europe and Japan, with one year's rates in the title.

    Draws Fig. 7 (inspired by Fig. 7.7 in Jones).

    Arguments
        year : the year marked by the dotted line and reported in the title
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the year's three rates (rates_in)
    row = rates_in(year)
    # Step 2: one line per economy
    fig = px.line(
        unemp,
        x="year",
        y=["United States", "Europe", "Japan"],
        labels={
            "year": "Year",
            "value": "Unemployment rate (percent)",
            "variable": "Economy",
        },
    )
    # Step 3: `add_vline` draws a vertical line at the chosen year
    fig.add_vline(x=year, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY)
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 14])
    # Step 4: the title reports the three rates; one hover box for all three lines
    fig.update_layout(
        title=(
            f"{year}: U.S. {row['United States']:.1f}%, Europe {row['Europe']:.1f}%, "
            f"Japan {row['Japan']:.1f}%"
        ),
        hovermode="x unified",
    )
    return fig
```

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- In 2022, U.S. unemployment was 3.6 percent and Japan's 2.6 percent, as in the textbook. Europe's was
  6.8 percent (the textbook's OECD series: 6.7).
- Until the late 1970s, Europe's rate was below the U.S. rate. It rose steeply between 1975 and 1985 and
  has stayed high since, with a peak of 12.1 percent in 2013.
- Japan's rate stayed low throughout. It was above the U.S. rate only in 1999–2001.

<!-- cell -->

#### Key numbers: Europe before and after 1975

```{python}
# The key numbers: average rates before 1975 and since 1985 (`&` means "and":
# both conditions must be true)
early = unemp[(unemp.year >= 1960) & (unemp.year <= 1975)]
late = unemp[unemp.year >= 1985]
print(
    "Average 1960-1975:",
    early[["United States", "Europe", "Japan"]].mean().round(2).to_dict(),
)
print(
    "Average 1985-2025:",
    late[["United States", "Europe", "Japan"]].mean().round(2).to_dict(),
)
# the years in which Europe, or Japan, had a higher rate than the U.S.
print(
    "First year with Europe above the U.S.:",
    unemp[unemp["Europe"] > unemp["United States"]].year.min(),
)
print(
    "Japan above the U.S. in:",
    unemp[unemp["Japan"] > unemp["United States"]].year.tolist(),
)
```

Up to 1975, Europe averaged 2.6 percent (the textbook says about 2.5), half the U.S. average. Since
1985 it has averaged about 9 percent, against under 6 percent in the United States. The textbook
explains the change with a mix of **adverse shocks** in the 1970s (the productivity slowdown and oil
prices) and **labor market institutions**, such as generous unemployment benefits, that kept
unemployment high once it had risen. In the bathtub model, both work through a lower job finding rate.

<!-- cell -->

#### Beyond three economies

"Europe" in the textbook's figure is an average. A wider file holds the annual unemployment rates of 42
countries from the same European Commission database (AMECO), for the EU members, other European
countries, and the United States, Japan, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Korea, plus the euro area
of 12 countries, the "Europe" line above.

```{python}
# Load the annual rates of 42 countries and the euro area, and look at Germany
# around reunification (rows 29 to 32 of its series)
ameco = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "unemployment_countries.csv")
ameco[ameco.country == "Germany"].iloc[29:33]
```

The rows show a **splice**: up to 1990 "Germany" is West Germany, and from 1991 the reunified country. Many
Central and Eastern European series start only in the 1990s or 2000s, after the end of communism.

First the data: `long_run_averages` picks the chosen countries and computes each one's
average rate since 1985, which the title reports.

```{python}
# The economies of the picker, A to Z, and the textbook's three
AMECO_COUNTRIES = sorted(ameco.country.unique())
BOOK_ECONOMIES = ("Euro area (12 countries)", "Japan", "United States")


def long_run_averages(names):
    """The rows of the chosen economies, and their average rates since 1985 (Fig. 7).

    Arguments
        names : the economies to show
    Returns
        chosen  : their rows of ameco
        average : each economy's average rate 1985-2025, from the lowest to the highest
    """
    # Step 1: the rows of the chosen economies
    chosen = ameco[ameco.country.isin(names)]
    if len(chosen) == 0:
        return chosen, None                    # nothing chosen: no averages
    # Step 2: one column per economy; `.loc[1985:2025]` keeps the rows from 1985 to
    # 2025, `.mean()` averages each column, and `.sort_values()` sorts the averages
    wide = chosen.pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="unemployment_rate")
    average = wide.loc[1985:2025].mean().sort_values()
    return chosen, average
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 7 for any economies
# the website's default view, and one fixed color per economy (group_colors)
AMECO_SHOWN = list(BOOK_ECONOMIES) + ["Spain", "South Korea"]
AMECO_COLORS = group_colors(
    AMECO_SHOWN + AMECO_COUNTRIES,
    [AMECO_SHOWN, AMECO_COUNTRIES],
    BOOK_COLORS,
)


def unemployment_long_run(names=BOOK_ECONOMIES):
    """Annual unemployment rates of any of 42 countries and the euro area.

    Draws Fig. 7 for any economies (inspired by Fig. 7.7 in Jones), with the highest
    and the lowest average since 1985 in the title.

    Arguments
        names : the economies to draw
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the data (long_run_averages); a message when nothing is picked
    chosen, average = long_run_averages(names)
    if len(chosen) == 0:
        return go.Figure(layout=dict(title="Pick at least one country"))
    # Step 2: the title; `.index[-1]` is the highest average, `.index[0]` the lowest
    title = f"Average 1985–2025: {average.index[-1]} {average.iloc[-1]:.1f}%"
    if len(average) > 1:
        title = title + (
            f" (highest), {average.index[0]} {average.iloc[0]:.1f}% (lowest)"
        )
    # Step 3: one line per economy, in its fixed color
    fig = px.line(
        chosen,
        x="year",
        y="unemployment_rate",
        color="country",
        hover_name="country",
        color_discrete_map=AMECO_COLORS,
        title=title,
        labels={
            "year": "Year",
            "unemployment_rate": "Unemployment rate (percent)",
            "country": "Economy",
        },
    )
    # Step 4: 0 to 14 percent, widened only for very high rates; no tick label in
    # the bottom-left corner; one hover box for all lines
    high = 14 if chosen.unemployment_rate.max() <= 14 else 40
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, high])
    fig.update_xaxes(tickvals=[1970, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010, 2020])
    fig.update_layout(hovermode="x unified")
    return fig
```

#### Table 7.2: hours worked per person

Hours worked per person combine three things: how many people work, how many weeks they work, and how
many hours a week. A wider file holds this measure from the Penn World Table, as an index with the U.S.
in 2019 = 100. Column `hours_pwt10` uses version 10.01, close to the textbook's version 10.0; column
`hours_pwt11` uses the latest version, 11.0.

```{python}
# Table 7.2. Step 1: the file, and the textbook's seven countries
hours = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "hours_per_person.csv")
countries = [
    "United States", "Italy", "France", "Germany", "U.K.", "Japan", "South Korea",
]
# Step 2: `.pivot(index="country", columns="year", values=...)` gives one row per
# country and one column per year; `.loc[countries, [1960, 1990, 2019]]` keeps
# the seven countries and three years
pwt10 = hours.pivot(index="country", columns="year", values="hours_pwt10")
pwt10 = pwt10.loc[countries, [1960, 1990, 2019]]
pwt11 = hours.pivot(index="country", columns="year", values="hours_pwt11")
pwt11 = pwt11.loc[countries, [1960, 1990, 2019, 2023]]
# Step 3: both versions, then the average of the four European countries in 2019
# (`.loc['Italy':'U.K.', 2019]` takes the rows from Italy to the U.K.)
print("PWT 10.01 (the textbook's table):")
print(pwt10.round(0))
print("\nPWT 11.0 (latest version):")
print(pwt11.round(1))
print(
    f"\nEurope (four countries) in 2019: PWT 10.01 "
    f"{pwt10.loc['Italy':'U.K.', 2019].mean():.1f}, "
    f"PWT 11.0 {pwt11.loc['Italy':'U.K.', 2019].mean():.1f}"
)
```

Version 10.01 reproduces every cell of the textbook's table. In 2019, Japan worked about 10 percent more
hours per person than the United States, and the four European countries about 86 percent of the U.S.
level on average, while in 1960 all four had worked more than Americans. The latest version revises
several countries down (the U.K. by about 9 points in 2019, Japan by 7), but the ranking is the same.

## The rising return to education

College graduates earn much more than high school graduates, even though there are more of them every year. The data show the gap, and the model explains it with shifts in demand and supply.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 8: College versus high school wages and employment

**Goal.** Document a key fact of the labor market: college graduates earn much more than high school
graduates, and the gap has grown while the number of college graduates rose.

The textbook uses private data from Acemoglu and Molina. We use the closest public series, from the
Economic Policy Institute (EPI), based on the Current Population Survey:

- the **college wage premium**: how much more college graduates earn per hour than high school graduates
  with similar gender, race, age and region, from 1979;
- the **share of employment** held by workers with a bachelor's or higher degree, from 1976. This is a
  different measure from the textbook's share of *hours*, which is about twice as high.

```{python}
# Load the data of Fig. 8: the college premium and the college share, by year
college = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig7-8.csv")
college.tail()
```

The premium comes in two versions. `college_premium_pct` is the percent gap: a value of 60 means college
graduates earn 60 percent more. `college_premium_log_pct` is the same gap in **log points**, $100 \ln(1 + \text{gap})$,
the unit economists usually plot (and the textbook uses). For small gaps the two are close; for large
gaps the log version is smaller. Let us check that the two columns agree:

```{python}
# The log version computed from the percent version: 100 ln(1 + gap)
check = 100 * np.log(1 + college.college_premium_pct / 100)
# the largest gap between the two (`.abs()`: the absolute value)
print(
    "Largest difference between the two versions: "
    f"{(check - college.college_premium_log_pct).abs().max():.2f} log points"
)
```

Before plotting, we give the columns readable names for the legend.

```{python}
# Readable column names for the legend: `.rename(columns={old: new})`
named = college.rename(
    columns={
        "college_premium_log_pct": "College wage premium (log points)",
        "college_share_employment_pct": "Share of employment with a college degree",
    }
)
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 8, the college premium and the college share
# Step 1: one line per column, blue and teal
fig = px.line(
    named,
    x="year",
    y=[
        "College wage premium (log points)",
        "Share of employment with a college degree",
    ],
    hover_name="year",
    color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, TEAL],
    labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Percent"},
    title="College graduates became more numerous and better paid at the same time",
)
# Step 2: 0 to 60 percent, the legend below the chart, one hover box for both lines
fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 60])
fig.update_layout(
    legend=dict(orientation="h", y=-0.2, yanchor="top"),
    legend_title_text="",
    hovermode="x unified",
)
fig.show()
```

**Sources.** Data: Economic Policy Institute, State of Working America Data Library, from the Current Population Survey:
[regression-adjusted hourly wage premium of college graduates](https://data.epi.org/wage_gaps/hourly_wage_premium_college/line/year/national/wage_premium_mean_reg_college/overall) and
[share of employment by education](https://data.epi.org/labor_force/labor_force_emp/line/year/national/dist_share_emp/education). They replace the textbook's private Acemoglu–Molina series.
Prepared file: [`data/ch07/fig7-8.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch07/fig7-8.csv)
(see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch07/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 7.8 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- The premium rose steeply in the 1980s and more slowly in the 1990s. Since 2000 it has moved between
  about 44 and 49 log points, and it has slipped since 2020.
- At the same time, the share of workers with a college degree more than doubled. More supply **and** a
  higher price: Fig. 9 shows how supply and demand can produce both.
- The textbook's lines start in 1963 and show a dip in the premium in the 1970s (Fig. 13 explains it).
  The public data start in 1979.

#### Beyond the United States

EPI's adjusted premium exists only for the United States. For other countries, the OECD publishes a
simpler measure every year: the earnings of full-time workers aged 25–64 with a bachelor's or higher degree,
relative to those with only upper secondary (high school) education, which counts as 100. It also publishes
the share of adults with such a degree. A wider file holds both for 48 countries, mostly from 2013.

```{python}
# Load the OECD file, and look at the last four U.S. rows
oecd_college = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "college_premium_countries.csv")
oecd_college[oecd_college.country == "United States"].tail(4)
```

`premium_log_points` turns the relative earnings into log points, $100 \ln(\text{relative earnings}/100)$,
the unit of the chart above. This measure is not adjusted for age, gender or region, so for the United States
it is about 14 log points above EPI's (61 against 46 in 2024). Compare countries with one measure at a time.
One value was dropped when the file was built: Slovakia's 3.5 for 2013, a unit error in the source.

First the data: `latest_premiums` picks the chosen countries' rows with a premium, and
each country's premium in its latest year, which the title reports.

```{python}
# The countries with earnings data, A to Z. `.dropna(subset=[...])` drops the rows
# where that column is empty
PREMIUM_COUNTRIES = sorted(
    oecd_college.dropna(subset=["premium_log_points"]).country.unique()
)


def latest_premiums(names):
    """The chosen countries' college premiums, and the latest one of each (Fig. 8).

    Arguments
        names : the countries to show
    Returns
        chosen : their rows of oecd_college that have a premium
        latest : each country's premium in its latest year, from the lowest
    """
    # Step 1: the rows of the chosen countries that have a premium
    chosen = oecd_college[oecd_college.country.isin(names)]
    chosen = chosen.dropna(subset=["premium_log_points"])
    if len(chosen) == 0:
        return chosen, None                    # nothing chosen: no premiums
    # Step 2: `.groupby("country").last()` keeps the last row of each country, its
    # latest year; then sort the premiums from the lowest to the highest
    latest = chosen.groupby("country").last().premium_log_points.sort_values()
    return chosen, latest
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 8 for OECD countries
# one fixed color per country; every line can be on at once ("All lines")
PREMIUM_COLORS = group_colors(PREMIUM_COUNTRIES, [PREMIUM_COUNTRIES], BOOK_COLORS)


def premium_countries(names=("United States",)):
    """The college premium of any countries (log points, full-time workers 25-64).

    Draws Fig. 8 for any OECD countries (inspired by Fig. 7.8 in Jones), with the
    highest and the lowest latest premium in the title.

    Arguments
        names : the countries to draw
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the data (latest_premiums); a message when no country is picked
    chosen, latest = latest_premiums(names)
    if len(chosen) == 0:
        return go.Figure(layout=dict(title="Pick at least one country"))
    # Step 2: the title, the highest premium first and the lowest second
    title = (
        f"College premium, latest year: {latest.index[-1]} "
        f"{latest.iloc[-1]:.0f} log points"
    )
    if len(latest) > 1:
        title = title + f", {latest.index[0]} {latest.iloc[0]:.0f}"
    # Step 3: one line per country, with a marker at each year of data
    fig = px.line(
        chosen,
        x="year",
        y="premium_log_points",
        color="country",
        hover_name="country",
        markers=True,
        color_discrete_map=PREMIUM_COLORS,
        title=title,
        labels={
            "year": "Year",
            "premium_log_points": "College premium (log points)",
            "country": "Country",
        },
    )
    # Step 4: 0 to 70, widened only for very high premiums; no tick label in the
    # bottom-left corner
    high = 70 if chosen.premium_log_points.max() <= 70 else 130
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, high])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1999, 2026], tickvals=[2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2025])
    return fig
```

#### Key numbers: present discounted value

To value a college degree we need a tool from the textbook's Section 7.6. A payment received $T$ years
from now is worth less than the same payment today, because money today can earn interest at rate $R$.
Its **present discounted value** is (equation 9)

$$pdv = \frac{\text{future value}}{(1 + R)^T}$$

For a payment that arrives every year for $n$ years, starting today, we add up the present values of
all the payments. The geometric-series formula gives the sum directly (equation 10):

$$pdv = \text{payment} \times \frac{1 - \left(\frac{1}{1+R}\right)^n}{1 - \frac{1}{1+R}}$$

```{python}
def pdv(payment, R, years):
    """The present value of a payment received every year, starting today.

    Equation (10), computed as a sum: payment / (1 + R)^t for t = 0, ..., years - 1

    Arguments
        payment : the yearly payment, in dollars
        R       : the interest rate
        years   : the number of yearly payments
    Returns
        the present discounted value of the stream, in dollars
    """
    # the loop adds one discounted payment per year, so we can check the formula;
    # `**` is a power: `(1 + R) ** t` is (1 + R)^t
    total = 0.0
    for t in range(years):                       # t = 0 is today, t = 1 next year, ...
        total = total + payment / (1 + R) ** t
    return total


# Four examples; `:,.0f` prints a number with thousands separators, no decimals
print(f"$1,000 in 5 years at R = 10%:          ${1000 / 1.10 ** 5:,.0f}")
print(f"$100 a year for 20 years at R = 10%:   ${pdv(100, 0.10, 20):,.0f}")
a = 1 / 1.10                                     # the discount factor of equation (10)
print(f"... and with the formula (10):         ${100 * (1 - a ** 20) / (1 - a):,.0f}")
print(f"$100,000 a year for 45 years at 3%:   ${pdv(100_000, 0.03, 45):,.0f}")
print(f"$30,000 a year for 45 years at 3%:    ${pdv(30_000, 0.03, 45):,.0f}")
```

The loop and the formula agree. A prize of \$1,000 in five years is worth \$621 today, and \$100 a year for
20 years is worth \$936, so the second prize is better. A working life of 45 years at \$100,000 a year is
worth about \$2.53 million today: in this sense a typical new worker is a millionaire. And the \$30,000 a
year that a college degree adds (\$90,000 instead of \$60,000) is worth about \$758,000, far more than four
years of tuition and lost earnings.

The chart shows why: each bar is one year's \$100,000 wage valued today. Distant wages count for less, but
they still add up. (`np.arange(45)` gives the whole numbers 0, 1, ..., 44.)

```{python}
# One bar per year: a wage of 100,000 dollars received t years from now is worth
# 100,000 / 1.03^t today (equation 9). `np.arange(45)` gives 0, 1, ..., 44
years = np.arange(45)
today = pd.DataFrame({"year": years, "value": 100_000 / 1.03 ** years})
```

```{python}

    x="year",
    y="value",
    hover_name="year",
    color_discrete_sequence=[TEAL],
    labels={"year": "Years from today", "value": "Value today (dollars)"},
    title=(
        "45 years of 100,000-dollar wages at R = 3% are worth "
        f"{today.value.sum():,.0f} dollars today"
    ),
```

chart uses no data. Inspired by the present-value discussion in Section 7.6 of Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

### Fig. 9: Understanding the rising return to education

**Goal.** See how the college wage can rise even though many more people go to college.

Fig. 8 showed both more college graduates and a higher college premium. In a supply-and-demand
diagram, more supply alone would *lower* the college wage. So demand for college graduates must have
shifted out too, and by more than supply. Panel (a) is the market for high school graduates, which we
keep unchanged. Panel (b) is the market for college graduates, with demand
$w = (90 + \text{shift}_d) - 0.4L$ and supply $w = (30 - \text{shift}_s) + 0.6L$. Before the shifts, the
college wage is 66 and the high school wage 55, a premium of 20 percent.

We draw the college market in a function of its own, because Fig. 13 uses it again. The curves before
the shifts are dashed gray ($L^s$, $L^d$) and the curves after them solid ($L^{s\prime}$, $L^{d\prime}$). The
equilibrium before the shifts is marked $*$ and the one after them $**$.

First the economics: `college_premium` solves the two markets of equation (3) and
gives the college premium over high school before and after the shifts.

```{python}
def college_premium(shift_d, shift_s):
    """The college wage and the premium over high school, before and after the shifts.

    Equation (3) for each market; the wage change follows equation (11). The high
    school market is Islandia's; the college market has demand w = (90 + shift_d)
    - 0.4 L and supply w = (30 - shift_s) + 0.6 L (Figs. 9 and 13).

    Arguments
        shift_d : how far college labor demand shifts out
        shift_s : how far college labor supply shifts out
    Returns
        w_hs           : the high school wage
        w_1, w_2       : the college wage before and after the shifts
        premium_1, premium_2 : the college premium before and after (0.2 = 20%)
    """
    # Step 1: the high school wage, and the college wage before and after
    w_hs = equilibrium()[1]
    w_1 = equilibrium(a_d=90.0, b_d=0.4, a_s=30.0, b_s=0.6)[1]
    w_2 = equilibrium(a_d=90.0 + shift_d, b_d=0.4, a_s=30.0 - shift_s, b_s=0.6)[1]
    # Step 2: the premium: how much more college graduates earn, as a share
    premium_1 = w_1 / w_hs - 1
    premium_2 = w_2 / w_hs - 1
    return w_hs, w_1, w_2, premium_1, premium_2
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Figs. 9 and 13, the college labor market
def college_market(fig, shift_d, shift_s, row=None, col=None):
    """The college labor market before (*) and after (**) both curves shift.

    Draws panel (b) of Fig. 9 and Fig. 13 (adapted from Figs. 7.9b and 7.13 in
    Jones): the curves before the shifts dashed gray, the curves after them solid.

    Arguments
        fig      : the figure to draw on
        shift_d  : how far college labor demand shifts out
        shift_s  : how far college labor supply shifts out
        row, col : the panel to draw in (None: the only panel)
    Returns
        w_1, w_2 : the college wage before and after the shifts
    """
    # Step 1: the equilibrium before and after the shifts, equation (3)
    L_1, w_1 = equilibrium(a_d=90.0, b_d=0.4, a_s=30.0, b_s=0.6)
    L_2, w_2 = equilibrium(a_d=90.0 + shift_d, b_d=0.4, a_s=30.0 - shift_s, b_s=0.6)
    # Step 2: the new curves solid, the old ones dashed gray
    supply = add_curve(
        fig, labor_supply(L_grid, 30.0 - shift_s, 0.6), "Lˢ′", TEAL, "solid", row, col
    )
    demand = add_curve(
        fig, labor_demand(L_grid, 90.0 + shift_d, 0.4), "Lᵈ′", BLUE, "solid", row, col,
        start=True,
    )
    add_curve(fig, labor_supply(L_grid, 30.0, 0.6), "Lˢ", GRAY, "dash", row, col,
              avoid=supply)
    add_curve(fig, labor_demand(L_grid, 90.0, 0.4), "Lᵈ", GRAY, "dash", row, col,
              start=True, avoid=demand)
    # Step 3: the two equilibria. `a or b` is true when at least one of the two is
    # true; with no shifts, ** is the same point as *
    add_point(fig, L_1, w_1, "*", row, col)
    if shift_d > 0 or shift_s > 0:
        add_point(fig, L_2, w_2, "**", row, col)
    return w_1, w_2
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 9, understanding the rising return to education
def rising_return(shift_d=15.0, shift_s=10.0):
    """(a) The high school market is unchanged; (b) college demand shifts out more.

    Draws Fig. 9 (adapted from Fig. 7.9 in Jones).

    Arguments
        shift_d : how far college labor demand shifts out
        shift_s : how far college labor supply shifts out
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the numbers of the figure (college_premium), and the high school market
    w_hs, w_1, w_2, premium_1, premium_2 = college_premium(shift_d, shift_s)
    L_hs = equilibrium()[0]
    # Step 2: `make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2)` makes two panels side by side; the
    # last two arguments of each drawing tool (here 1, 1) say which panel to use
    fig = make_subplots(
        rows=1,
        cols=2,
        subplot_titles=("(a) High school graduates", "(b) College graduates"),
    )
    # Step 3: panel (a), the high school market
    add_curve(fig, labor_supply(L_grid), "Lˢ", TEAL, "solid", 1, 1)
    add_curve(fig, labor_demand(L_grid), "Lᵈ", BLUE, "solid", 1, 1, start=True)
    add_point(fig, L_hs, w_hs, "*", 1, 1)
    # Step 4: panel (b), the college market (college_market)
    college_market(fig, shift_d, shift_s, 1, 2)
    title = (
        f"College wage {w_1:.1f} → {w_2:.1f}; premium over high school "
        f"{premium_1:.0%} → {premium_2:.0%}"
    )
    return market_axes(fig, title, x_title="Employment", y_title="Wage")
```

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- With the default shifts, college employment rises from 60 to 85 **and** the college wage rises from 66 to
  71. The premium over high school graduates rises from 20 to 29 percent.
- Set the demand shift to 0: the extra supply alone lowers the college wage. The rising premium needs a
  large shift in demand.
- Two explanations for that shift are **skill-biased technical change** (computers and software make
  skilled workers more productive) and **globalization** (trade with countries where skilled workers are
  scarce raises their value; trade with countries rich in unskilled labor lowers the wages of the unskilled).

Prepared files: [`data/ch07/fig7-10.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch07/fig7-10.csv), [`data/ch07/recessions.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch07/recessions.csv)
(see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch07/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 7.10 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- Manufacturing employment grew until the late 1970s, fell in every recession, and was roughly flat in the
  1990s.
- From 2000 to 2010 it dropped by about a third and never recovered.
- Research the textbook cites finds that rising imports from China explain about a quarter of that decline.

<!-- cell -->

#### Key numbers: the fall after 2000

```{python}
# The key numbers of Fig. 10: the series with the months as row labels, and its
# lowest point between 2000 and 2012
m = manuf.set_index("date").manufacturing_emp_millions
low = m.loc["2000":"2012"]
fall = m.loc["2000-01-01"] - low.min()
print(f"Peak: {m.max():.2f} million in {m.idxmax():%B %Y}")
print(
    f"January 2000: {m.loc['2000-01-01']:.2f} million;  "
    f"low: {low.min():.2f} million in {low.idxmin():%B %Y}"
)
# the fall after 2000, and the quarter of it linked to imports from China
print(
    f"Fall: {fall:.2f} million ({fall / m.loc['2000-01-01']:.0%});  "
    f"a quarter of it: {fall / 4:.2f} million jobs"
)
print(f"Latest: {m.iloc[-1]:.2f} million in {m.index[-1]:%B %Y}")
```

Between January 2000 and February 2010 the sector lost 5.84 million jobs, 34 percent of its employment.
A quarter of that, the share linked to Chinese imports, is about 1.5 million jobs.

#### Beyond the United States

The ILO estimates employment in manufacturing for almost every country since 1991, from labor surveys. A
wider file holds the number of manufacturing workers (millions) and their share of all employed people.

```{python}
# Load the ILO estimates, and look at the last three U.S. rows
manuf_world = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "manufacturing_countries.csv")
manuf_world[manuf_world.country == "United States"].tail(3)
```

The ILO counts 16.2 million U.S. manufacturing workers in 2025, about 3.5 million more than the payroll
count above, because household surveys also count the self-employed and people whose employer is classified
elsewhere. Different sources, different levels: compare **shares** across countries, and compare levels
only within one source. A few series end before 2025 (Ukraine in 2021, Sudan in 2022).

First the data: `manufacturing_change` picks the chosen countries and computes each
one's change since 1991, in the measure you choose, which the title reports.

```{python}
# Step 1: the countries of the picker, A to Z, and each country's region
MANUF_COUNTRIES = sorted(manuf_world.country.unique())
MANUF_REGIONS = dict(zip(manuf_world.country, manuf_world.region))
# Step 2: `MEASURES` is a dictionary of lists: for each choice of the buttons, the
# column to plot, its axis title, the usual and the wider axis top, and the unit
MEASURES = {
    "share of jobs": [
        "manufacturing_share", "Manufacturing, % of all jobs", 30, 40, "points",
    ],
    "millions of workers": [
        "manufacturing_millions", "Manufacturing workers (millions)",
        25, 180, "million",
    ],
}


def manufacturing_change(names, measure):
    """The chosen countries' rows, and each one's change since 1991 (Fig. 10).

    Arguments
        names   : the countries to show
        measure : "share of jobs" or "millions of workers"
    Returns
        chosen : their rows of manuf_world
        change : each country's change from its first to its last year, sorted
    """
    # Step 1: the rows of the chosen countries, and the column of the measure
    chosen = manuf_world[manuf_world.country.isin(names)]
    column = MEASURES[measure][0]
    if len(chosen) == 0:
        return chosen, None                    # nothing chosen: no change
    # Step 2: the last year minus the first year of each country
    by_country = chosen.groupby("country")
    change = (by_country.last()[column] - by_country.first()[column]).sort_values()
    return chosen, change
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 10 for any countries
# the website's default view, and one fixed color per country (group_colors)
MANUF_SHOWN = ["United States", "Germany", "Vietnam"]
MANUF_COLORS = group_colors(
    MANUF_SHOWN + MANUF_COUNTRIES,
    region_groups(MANUF_REGIONS, MANUF_SHOWN),
    BOOK_COLORS,
)


def manufacturing_countries(names=("United States",), measure="share of jobs"):
    """Manufacturing employment of any countries (ILO): a share of jobs, or millions.

    Draws Fig. 10 for any countries (inspired by Fig. 7.10 in Jones), with the
    largest fall and the largest rise since 1991 in the title.

    Arguments
        names   : the countries to draw
        measure : "share of jobs" or "millions of workers"
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the data (manufacturing_change); a message when no country is picked
    chosen, change = manufacturing_change(names, measure)
    if len(chosen) == 0:
        return go.Figure(layout=dict(title="Pick at least one country"))
    # Step 2: `column, label, high, wider, unit = MEASURES[measure]` unpacks the
    # five items of one list into five variables
    column, label, high, wider, unit = MEASURES[measure]
    # Step 3: the title, the largest fall first; `round(...) + 0.0` avoids "-0.0"
    title = (
        f"Change since 1991 ({unit}): "
        f"{change.index[0]} {round(change.iloc[0], 1) + 0.0:+.1f}"
    )
    if len(change) > 1:
        title = title + f", {change.index[-1]} {round(change.iloc[-1], 1) + 0.0:+.1f}"
    # Step 4: one line per country, in its fixed color
    fig = px.line(
        chosen,
        x="year",
        y=column,
        color="country",
        hover_name="country",
        color_discrete_map=MANUF_COLORS,
        title=title,
        labels={"year": "Year", column: label, "country": "Country"},
    )
    # Step 5: one wider range, only when a country needs it
    if chosen[column].max() > high:
        high = wider
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, high])
    return fig
```

### Fig. 11: Income inequality in the United States and France

**Goal.** Follow a century of top incomes in two countries.

The file gives the share of national income (before taxes and benefits) received by the richest 0.1
percent of adults, the top 1 in 1,000, from the World Inequality Database. These data come from tax records,
which show the very top of the distribution well.

```{python}
# Load the data of Fig. 11, and give the columns the countries' names
top = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig7-11.csv")
top = top.rename(
    columns={"top01_share_us": "United States", "top01_share_france": "France"}
)
top.tail()
```

Look at the last rows. France stops in 2022, and the U.S. value is exactly 9.93 in 2022, 2023 and 2024. Three
identical values in a row are unusual for an economic series: the database seems to repeat its last estimate
until new tax data arrive. We keep the rows but treat 2023–2024 with care.

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 11, top incomes in the United States and France
# Step 1: one line per country
fig = px.line(
    top,
    x="year",
    y=["United States", "France"],
    hover_name="year",
    labels={
        "year": "Year",
        "value": "Income share of the top 0.1% (percent)",
        "variable": "Country",
    },
    title=(
        "Top incomes fell after 1929 in both countries, "
        "but rose again only in the U.S."
    ),
)
# Step 2: 0 to 12 percent, and one hover box for both lines
fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 12])
fig.update_layout(hovermode="x unified")
fig.show()
```

**Sources.** Data: [World Inequality Database (WID)](https://wid.world/data/), share of pre-tax national income of the top 0.1 percent,
via [Our World in Data](https://ourworldindata.org/economic-inequality); WID extends the tax-record series of
Piketty and Saez (2003).
Prepared file: [`data/ch07/fig7-11.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch07/fig7-11.csv)
(see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch07/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 7.11 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- From 1913 to 1929 the top 0.1 percent received about 9 percent of all income on average in both
  countries, and more than 10 percent in peak years (the textbook says about 10 percent).
- The Great Depression and World War II cut their share sharply, and it stayed low until about 1980.
- After 1980 the U.S. share rose back to almost 10 percent, while France's stayed much lower.

<!-- cell -->

#### Key numbers: three eras

```{python}
# The average share of each era, in both countries
for start, end in [[1913, 1929], [1950, 1959], [1960, 1979], [2015, 2022]]:
    era = top[(top.year >= start) & (top.year <= end)]
    print(
        f"{start}-{end}: U.S. {era['United States'].mean():.1f}%, "
        f"France {era['France'].mean():.1f}%"
    )
```

The 1950s average is 5.0 percent in the United States and 3.7 in France; the textbook's "around 4
percent" fits the 1960s and 1970s better. Today's data also differ from the textbook's figure in two
places: a U.S. spike in 1950 (7.25 percent) and a higher French share after 2015 (5.56 percent in 2021,
against about 2.8 in the textbook). The database is revised as new tax records are added.

#### Beyond two countries

The World Inequality Database (WID) publishes the same top income shares for many countries. A wider file
holds the share of the top 0.1 percent for 58 countries: the 38 OECD members and 20 large emerging
economies.

```{python}
# Load the WID file, and look at Brazil's first twelve rows
top_world = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "top01_share_countries.csv")
top_world[top_world.country == "Brazil"].head(12)
```

**Look at your data.** Every country has a value for every year since 1980. Before 1980, about 30 countries
have long series from tax records, like the United States and France. The others, like Brazil above, have
only a few *benchmark* years from WID's historical estimates (1820, 1850, 1880, 1900, 1910, ...), and a
line chart joins them with straight segments that hide everything in between. In the latest year, WID
repeats its previous estimate for 56 of the 58 countries. The chart starts in 1900 and marks each data point.

First the data: `top_share_latest` picks the chosen countries since 1900 and each one's
share in the latest year, which the title reports.

```{python}
# The countries of the picker, A to Z, each country's region, and the textbook's two
TOP_COUNTRIES = sorted(top_world.country.unique())
TOP_REGIONS = dict(zip(top_world.country, top_world.region))
BOOK_PAIR = ("France", "United States")


def top_share_latest(names):
    """The chosen countries' top 0.1% shares since 1900, and the latest ones (Fig. 11).

    Arguments
        names : the countries to show
    Returns
        chosen : their rows of top_world from 1900 on
        last   : the latest year of those rows
        latest : each country's share in that year, from the lowest to the highest
    """
    # Step 1: the rows of the chosen countries from 1900 on (`&`: both must be true)
    chosen = top_world[top_world.country.isin(names) & (top_world.year >= 1900)]
    # Step 2: the latest year, and each country's share in it, sorted
    last = chosen.year.max()
    latest = chosen[chosen.year == last].set_index("country").top01_share.sort_values()
    return chosen, last, latest
```

```{python}
#| kind: drawing
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 11 for any countries
# one fixed color per country (group_colors)
TOP_COLORS = group_colors(
    TOP_COUNTRIES,
    region_groups(TOP_REGIONS, BOOK_PAIR),
    BOOK_COLORS,
)


def top_share_countries(names=BOOK_PAIR):
    """The income share of the top 0.1% of any countries since 1900 (WID).

    Draws Fig. 11 for any countries (inspired by Fig. 7.11 in Jones), with the
    highest and the lowest share of the latest year in the title.

    Arguments
        names : the countries to draw
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the data (top_share_latest); a message when no country is picked
    chosen, last, latest = top_share_latest(names)
    if len(chosen) == 0:
        return go.Figure(layout=dict(title="Pick at least one country"))
    # Step 2: the title, the highest share first and the lowest second
    title = (
        f"Top 0.1% income share in {last}: "
        f"{latest.index[-1]} {latest.iloc[-1]:.1f}%"
    )
    if len(latest) > 1:
        title = title + f" (highest), {latest.index[0]} {latest.iloc[0]:.1f}% (lowest)"
    # Step 3: one line per country, with a small marker at each data point
    fig = px.line(
        chosen,
        x="year",
        y="top01_share",
        color="country",
        hover_name="country",
        markers=True,
        color_discrete_map=TOP_COLORS,
        title=title,
        labels={
            "year": "Year",
            "top01_share": "Income share of the top 0.1% (percent)",
            "country": "Country",
        },
    )
    fig.update_traces(marker=dict(size=4))
    # Step 4: 0 to 16 percent, widened only for very high shares; no tick label in
    # the bottom-left corner
    high = 16 if chosen.top01_share.max() <= 16 else 25
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, high])
    fig.update_xaxes(
        range=[1898, 2026],
        tickvals=[1920, 1940, 1960, 1980, 2000, 2020],
    )
    return fig
```
